extracted.intended_audience: Mathematics instructors (K–12 and postsecondary), course designers, and teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_short: assessment and feedback in math teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and implementing assessment, feedback, peer-assessment, and grading practices in mathematics courses to support learning rather than sorting. Emphasizes formative assessment strategies, feedback types, peer/self assessment routines, and decoupling grades from feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment communicates what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment is one of the primary mechanisms through which we communicate “what counts” in a mathematics classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose meaningful problems and ensure linguistic, cultural, and other elements of tasks are accessible to all students. The quality of assessments is closely related to the quality of tasks selected; providing a wider variety of ways for students to express understanding expands what it means to understand mathematics. See Section 4.4.1 for how to choose good tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish assessment, feedback, and grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment allows us to surface student thinking and generate feedback; grading is primarily a mechanism to create and sustain hierarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disentangle grading and feedback as much as possible. Use assessment to provide evidence for student understanding and to generate feedback that students can act on; avoid letting high-stakes grades be the primary way students receive feedback because grades can undermine the uptake of comments and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer formative assessment (assessment for learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative assessment practices help surface what students do and do not understand, how they are thinking, and where they are getting stuck; they are called assessment for learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement formative assessment strategies regularly so instructors can adapt instruction and students can use feedback to revise their learning. Formative practices (including peer- and self-assessment) show small-to-medium positive effects on learning; student-initiated formative assessment has larger effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use questioning strategically to probe thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: When we ask questions with attention to student thinking, classroom discussion can provide a window into student understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions of many students (not just a few), treat yourself as a detective probing understanding rather than a judge getting the right answer, and plan questions before lessons to surface student thinking and identify areas for growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface in-progress thinking via rough drafts and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic mathematics is messy; to understand how students are grappling with ideas you must surface in-progress work (rough drafts) and provide exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whiteboards, have students bring rough drafts before turning in homework, gather anonymous class samples of varying quality, and expose students to exemplars after they produce drafts. Provide opportunities for revision (peer-feedback, assignment revisions, test corrections) to build a culture of revision and productive struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opening problems as diagnostic entry points
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin class with a short opening problem that transitions students into 'math mode' and reveals prior understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening problems can preview the day's content or review prior lessons, provide diagnostic information to adjust instruction that day, and create opportunities for engagement and feedback early in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exit tickets to check uptake and prompt reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Exit tickets are short end-of-class tasks that reveal how the lesson was received and can prompt reflective writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask brief conceptual questions or a short problem related to the lesson; sample prompts: 'What was a key takeaway?', 'What questions do you have?', 'Is there anything else I should know?'. Use responses to inform subsequent instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage classroom strategies as formative assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many active-learning strategies can double as formative assessment when used to surface student thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques such as think-pair-share, gallery walks, paper toss, student presentations, and everyone-shares can be used to gather information about student understanding that is then used to revise instruction or guide student self-assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback should be agentive and interpretable by learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback is a process in which learners make sense of information about their performance and use it to enhance the quality of their work or learning strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center learners as active agents; ensure tasks and learning environment generate usable feedback throughout the process, not just after completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build capacity, design, and culture for feedback (Henderson guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective feedback systems require attention to (a) capacity for feedback, (b) designs for feedback, and (c) culture for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity for feedback: learners and educators understand and value feedback; learners are active; educators seek and use evidence; access to appropriate space/technology. Designs for feedback: information is usable and learners know how to use it; tailored to learner needs; variety of sources/modes; alignment of learning outcomes. Culture for feedback: feedback is valued and visible; processes ensure consistency/quality; leadership ensures continuity of vision; educators have flexibility to deploy resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide high-information competence feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence feedback provides detailed information about what students are doing and why it is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific strengths and explain exactly why they matter (e.g., 'I noticed you used the theorems we just discussed; this seems productive.'), which supports student confidence, positions them as mathematicians, and guides future work. Consider whether feedback is public or private as that affects positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty praise as primary feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Empty praise focuses learners on themselves and performance and can inhibit learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common empty praise (e.g., 'Awesome!', 'You’re a math genius!') shifts attention from task to self and can promote performance orientation. If praise is given, pair it with competence feedback that explains what was done well; better yet, focus on growth-oriented statements about effort and persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give growth-focused feedback (specific, actionable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth feedback provides specific information about areas to improve on a task—how and why—so learners can learn to do the task better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on task, processes, and reasoning (not global judgments). Provide concrete suggestions (e.g., point out gaps in argument, suggest use of theorems or diagrams), and structure opportunities for revision so feedback can be acted upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wise feedback when giving critical feedback to minoritized students
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise feedback couples specific critical feedback with an explicit invocation of high standards and assurance of the student's capability to meet them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three features: (1) specific critical feedback, (2) explicit high standards, (3) assurance the student can meet standards. Frame critiques to signal belief in the student's ability and provide concrete steps to improve to reduce stereotype-threat or mentor’s-dilemma effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple grades from feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Grades focus learners on performance and can eliminate the learning benefits of written comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pairing grades with comments; provide feedback without a grade and allow revision before assigning grades. When comments are paired with grades, students often ignore the comments and the grades undermine intrinsic motivation. Use alternatives to traditional grading to maintain feedback usefulness (see Section 6.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Activate students via peer- and self-assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer- and self-assessment foster independence, interdependence, and abundant feedback beyond what instructors alone can provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize activities so students analyze peer work, provide feedback, receive feedback, conference, and revise. Peer assessment helps students develop a concept of high-quality work and evaluative judgment, and can improve performance even if peers have less expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement an assessment cycle with explicit steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment cycle involves analyzing peer work, providing feedback to peers, receiving feedback, conferencing, and revising one's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step affords different learning opportunities: analyzing peer work builds evaluative judgment, providing feedback develops critical lenses, and revision allows incorporation of input. Use the cycle to develop feedback literacies and self-assessment skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach self-assessment component skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-assessment requires understanding learning criteria, gathering feedback, and reflecting on skills relative to feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must be taught how to interpret criteria, discriminate useful vs. irrelevant feedback, and reflect; without such instruction self-assessment can fail, partly due to biases like the Dunning–Kruger effect. Use peer-assessment to help students practice these skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide varied-quality examples for assessment training
rubrics_metrics.description: Students learn self-assessment better from examples of work that vary in quality rather than only from expert, flawless solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a range of student or prior-semester samples (including partially correct work) to have students grapple with judgment tasks; assessing peer work helps them learn to identify gaps and standards they can apply to their own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured peer-feedback routines (Peer-Assisted Reflection, PAR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-Assisted Reflection (PAR) is a structured routine for peer feedback that can be incorporated into independent problem-solving and homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAR has been used across contexts (intro calculus to graduate analysis) and is flexible; studies report increased passing rates and effect sizes for explanation improvements. Implement PAR procedures (e.g., exchange drafts, provide structured feedback prompts, revise work) to catalyze peer- and self-assessment.
